clue.text: Refs abused after boy band's sporting feats

indicators.note: Letters that have been abused have been knocked about, so they come out in an order other than the one they were handed over in.
After sends the word in front of it to the back, so the knocked-about letters follow the band rather than opening the entry.

parts.note: Five were the British boy band of the late nineties who put their name on records as 5ive
four letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Match officials taking abuse in the wake of a boy band's athletic triumphs.
explanation.walkthrough: A five-fer is cricket's shorthand for a bowler taking five wickets in an innings, spelt the way commentators say it. The hyphen in the enumeration is the clue's one honest signal that a number starts the entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Five-fers are hauls of five wickets in an innings, which is the kind of performance a scorecard records as a feat.

clue.text: See 15
A couple short of a dozen legs — and joints?

parts.words: A couple short of a dozen
parts.note: a dozen is twelve and a couple is two, so the arithmetic is done in words
in cricket the leg side of the wicket is also called the on side, so a leg is an on

explanation.surface: Counting up a creature that has two fewer than twelve legs, and wondering about its joints.
explanation.walkthrough: A tenon is the tongue of wood cut to fit a mortise, so the joints are carpentry rather than anatomy. Cricket's on side is the side the batter's legs stand on, which lets one word stand in for the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Tenons are the projecting tongues cut on a timber's end to slot into mortises, the joint that holds a frame or a chair together.

clue.text: Burns fumes about cigar's end

indicators.note: Something placed about a thing is wrapped round it, so the letter named next goes into the middle.

parts.note: a kettle or a hot road fumes in the sense of giving off vapour

indicators.note: The end of a word is where its final letter sits, so only that one letter is taken.

parts.note: the last letter of cigar

explanation.surface: A man called Burns in a temper because his cigar has gone down to the stub.
explanation.walkthrough: A burn is a Scottish brook, which is why the capital B at the head of the clue can pretend to be a surname. 'Fumes' works twice over: rage on the surface, vapour underneath.
explanation.definitionFit: Burns are the small watercourses of Scotland and northern England, so the plural noun and the answer name the same running water.

clue.text: See 22
Special few a part of ménages à trois?

parts.note: count the phrases standing in a row in front of the definition: there are three of them
and every one of the three says the same word — some as in 'that's some car', some as in a few, some as in a portion

explanation.surface: A particular handful of people making up part of a French three-cornered arrangement.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay counts words instead of letters, which is why nothing in it looks like fodder. 'Special' is the some of 'that's some car', and once all three openers are seen to be saying one word, their number supplies the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A ménage à trois is a household of three people sharing a relationship, which is one sense of a threesome, and the French plural matches the plural answer.

clue.text: Scratching surface of dark side in barrel

indicators.note: What is in something sits inside it, so these letters are dropped into the middle of the word named next.

parts.note: a keg is the small barrel beer is drawn from
in Chinese thought yin is the dark, shadowed half of the pair whose other half is yang

explanation.surface: Only beginning to look into the sinister business kept in a barrel.
explanation.walkthrough: To key a car is to drag a key along its paintwork, which is scratching a surface in the most deliberate way there is. 'Dark side' belongs to yin and yang, not to a villain.
explanation.definitionFit: Keying means dragging something sharp along paintwork, so the answer is the act of scratching a surface rather than a synonym for damage.

clue.text: Painstaking papers back essentially glib man

indicators.note: back means the papers abbreviation is read in reverse

parts.note: ID means identity papers

indicators.note: essentially points to the core of glib, its two middle letters

parts.note: its middle letters are LI
a gent is a man

explanation.surface: A careful worker turns the newspapers over, deep down a smooth talker.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'papers back' as someone reading the back pages; it is identity papers turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone diligent is hard-working and takes great care, which is what painstaking describes.

clue.text: Badenoch reveals strain — of iron?

indicators.note: to strain is to filter something out, so the answer is sieved out of the run of letters in Badenoch reveals

parts.note: the letters run across the end of Badenoch and the start of reveals

explanation.surface: The politician Kemi Badenoch admits to feeling the strain, perhaps as the 'Iron Lady' successor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reveals' looks like the signal, but it is part of the fodder: the answer straddles BadenOCH REveals, and 'strain' does the filtering. Kemi Badenoch is a leader of the UK Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: Ochre is an earthy pigment coloured by iron oxide, so it is literally a thing made of iron; the question mark admits the stretch.

clue.text: Stable houses setter — was one lost?

parts.note: the setter is the person writing the puzzle, who refers to himself as me

indicators.note: What is lost is no longer among the letters, so the piece named beside it drops out of the word it was in.

parts.note: three letters, taken as they stand
a is the article that means one, as in a dozen for one dozen

explanation.surface: A stable with a setter living in it, and the question of whether one has gone missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter is the compiler signing himself in, not the gun dog the stable invites you to picture. Losing 'one' means losing an A, which is the commonest way a clue asks for that letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A mews is a row of old stables converted into dwellings, so the plural noun names stables and houses in one breath.

clue.text: Regarding those unidentified, technology goes too far

parts.note: a row over money is a row regarding money, so over can mean concerning
an unidentified person in an American court is a John or a Jane Doe, so several of them are Does
IT is information technology, the department that mends the laptops

explanation.surface: A memo about unidentified persons, complaining that the technology has got out of hand.
explanation.walkthrough: John Doe and Jane Doe are the American names for people whose identity is unknown, so more than one of them is a plural. 'Over' here is the preposition meaning concerning, the sense in 'an argument over money'.
explanation.definitionFit: To overdo it is to push something past the sensible point, which is what going too far describes.

clue.text: Savages live, pasts quietly forgotten

parts.note: to be is to live, as in let me be

indicators.note: What has been forgotten is no longer there, so the letter named beside it goes missing from the word before.

parts.note: five letters, the word the deletion works on
p is piano on a score, the instruction to play softly

explanation.surface: Savage men still alive, their histories conveniently forgotten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Savages' looks like the verb a critic does to a book and is in fact the noun, the wild things themselves. Piano is the softest marking a composer writes, which is why quiet is p in hundreds of clues.
explanation.definitionFit: Beasts are wild animals and, said of people, brutes, which is exactly the plural noun savages names.

clue.text: Here solstice worshipping teens go wild, gobbling bird

definitions.note: The definition is locative rather than a noun: the answer names the place where solstice worship happens, with 'here' pointing at it and the rest saying which place is meant.

indicators.note: Letters told to go wild stop behaving, and they will not come back in the order they were given.
To gobble a thing is to swallow it whole, so what is named next is taken inside.

parts.note: seven letters shuffled, and they part in the middle to take the bird
a hen is the female of the farmyard bird

explanation.surface: Teenagers who worship the solstice running riot at a spot, wolfing down poultry.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface paints the midsummer crowd at a stone circle and the answer is that circle, so picture and place turn out to be one. 'Gobbling' has to be swallowing here, never the noise a turkey makes.
explanation.definitionFit: Stonehenge is the Wiltshire circle where crowds gather to watch the sun come up at midsummer, so 'here' is pointing straight at it.

clue.text: Video game reversed practice: that's not right

indicators.note: reversed means the word for the video game is read from its end

parts.note: a sim is a simulation video game, as in The Sims
usage is customary practice

explanation.surface: A gamer's play backfires, and someone protests that it is wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: The sim is a genre of video game, as in The Sims; the colon makes 'practice' look like part of the definition, but it supplies the last five letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Misusage is wrong or improper use, so the word labels something that is incorrect.

clue.text: Golden age — at end of festivities?

wordplay.reading: the tail of festivities after FESTI, with VI a Roman numeral spelt out

parts.note: the closing letters of festivities, after FESTI, are a Roman numeral followed by the letters for neckwear knots, and the numeral is then written out in words

explanation.surface: A glorious era comes, perhaps, once the party is over.
explanation.walkthrough: The end of festivities reads VI TIES. In this numbers-themed puzzle the Roman numeral VI is spelt out as SIX, and the question mark flags that sleight of hand.
explanation.definitionFit: The Swinging Sixties are often looked back on as a golden era of music, fashion and freedom.

clue.text: Drugs cost (including recipe) negotiable for gigolos

indicators.note: Including throws the letter named next in among the others, so it joins the pool waiting to be shuffled.

parts.note: e is ecstasy, so more than one tablet is Es

indicators.note: A price that is negotiable can be moved about, and so can the letters the word is standing beside.

parts.note: four letters waiting to be rearranged
r stands for recipe, the Latin instruction written at the head of a prescription

explanation.surface: A street price for drugs with the recipe thrown in, open to haggling by men who sell company.
explanation.walkthrough: Escort is the trade's polite word for someone paid for their company, and the definition only makes it male. The bracket is not decoration: it says the odd letter joins the others before any shuffling happens.
explanation.definitionFit: Gigolos are men paid to squire women about, which is what male escorts advertise themselves as doing.

clue.text: These world leaders on Russian river? It's … it's worth little in America

definitions.note: Two bits is a noun, an American quarter, while the definition talks about worth: it is pointing at the idiom in which anything two-bit is dismissed as trifling.

indicators.note: The leaders of words are the letters at their head, so one letter is taken from the front of each.

parts.note: the opening letter of each word of the pair
the Ob is one of the great Siberian rivers, flowing north into the Arctic
the apostrophe is dropped, as crossword spelling always allows

explanation.surface: World leaders meeting on a Russian river, and a shrug about how little the whole thing is worth.
explanation.walkthrough: Two bits is twenty-five cents — a bit was an eighth of a Spanish dollar — so the phrase is American for small change. The row of dots is the surface trailing off and hides nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Two bits is American slang for a quarter, and anything called two-bit over there is being dismissed as cheap.

clue.text: Excuses politician embraced by alien in sex romp

indicators.note: To be embraced is to be held with arms either side, so these letters go inside the ones named next.

parts.note: three letters shuffled into a wrapper that opens after the first two

indicators.note: In puts what has been assembled so far inside the letters that follow.
A romp is a boisterous tumble, and letters that have been tumbled do not land in their old order.

parts.note: ET has been the crossword extraterrestrial since the film
an MP is a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A politician caught in an alien's arms during a sex romp.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Excuses' is the verb — what a tax rule does for you — rather than the noun a schoolboy offers. The wrapping happens twice, the smaller parcel going inside the bigger one before anything else is read.
explanation.definitionFit: To exempt somebody is to let them off a duty everyone else has to meet, which is what excusing them from it amounts to.

clue.text: Settlers erected timber frames

indicators.note: Erected means put up out of parts, and a thing built from the same parts stands in a different arrangement.

parts.note: eight letters waiting to be built up again

explanation.surface: Pioneers putting up wooden structures at their new settlement.
explanation.walkthrough: Trestles are the splayed wooden legs a plank rests on — a pasting table stands on a pair. The difficulty is that fodder and definition sit flush against each other with only the instruction between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A trestle is a braced wooden frame, and two of them under a board make a table, so timber frames names them plainly.

clue.text: Confused? Yes — call in dope dispenser

indicators.note: in means the word for call goes inside the jumbled letters
confused suggests the word yes is muddled, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: to ring someone is to call them on the phone

explanation.surface: Someone bewildered agrees to phone a drug supplier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Confused' rearranges yes, and 'in' puts the call inside. Dope here means a drug, which this device dispenses.
explanation.definitionFit: A syringe is a device for injecting fluids, so it delivers a dose of a drug.

clue.text: Otherwise show one mercy in service

indicators.note: Otherwise means in some other way, and letters taken another way are letters taken in another order.

parts.note: three letters of the fodder
and the five that complete it

explanation.surface: A plea for somebody to be shown mercy in the middle of a church service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Show one mercy' is a whole idiom on the surface and no more than a bag of letters underneath. A service is a ceremony whether it is a wedding, a funeral or a christening.
explanation.definitionFit: A service — wedding, funeral, memorial — is a formal ceremony, so the two nouns name the same occasion.

clue.text: England collapse over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over

definitions.text: over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over

parts.note: a cricket team has a fixed number of players, which is why a national side is named by that number
a business that collapses, or a poker player giving up a hand, is said to do this

explanation.surface: England's batting caving in over after over after over.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is not described but performed: count the repetitions and the number is the one the entry opens with. An over is six balls of cricket, which is what makes the collapse funny.
explanation.definitionFit: Anything done over and over eleven times has happened elevenfold, so the printed repetition acts the definition out instead of stating it.

clue.text: Revelling used to put out

indicators.note: To revel is to carouse without restraint, and letters doing that will not keep to their places.

parts.note: four letters of the fodder
and the two that finish it

explanation.surface: Partying that once had a habit of annoying the neighbours.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put out' carries three senses worth trying — annoyed, extinguished and thrown out — and the entry wants the third. The fodder is the everyday phrase standing in front of it, which reads as tense rather than letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To oust somebody is to drive them from a post or a property, so a leader who has been ousted has been put out of office.

clue.text: 'Aussie' (not American) nightwear

wordplay.reading: AUSSIE without US, its A spelt out as a number

parts.note: Aussie is A plus US plus SIE; dropping the American US leaves A and SIE, and A, which means one as in 'a dozen', is written out as the number

explanation.surface: An Australian, explicitly not a Yank, gets into pyjamas.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking US (American) out of AUSSIE leaves A SIE. In this numbers-themed puzzle A, meaning one, is spelt out as ONE, giving ONE SIE.
explanation.definitionFit: A onesie is a loose one-piece garment, often worn for lounging or sleeping.

clue.text: Football seen around half ten, with commentary for audience

indicators.note: What goes around a thing is wrapped about it, so the letter named next lands in the middle.
Half is one of two equal parts, and the number beside it is the Roman numeral, a character that splits cleanly down the middle.

parts.note: four letters that open in the middle
ten in Roman numerals is X, and the top or bottom half of that character is V, the Roman five
an aside is the remark an actor turns and delivers to the audience over the other characters' heads

explanation.surface: A football match caught at about half past ten, with commentary laid on for the crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half ten' is a time of day on the surface and half a Roman numeral underneath, which is the whole of the clue's trick. Seven-a-side is the short-pitch game, played with four fewer than a full team.
explanation.definitionFit: Seven-a-side is football played with seven to a team instead of eleven, so the answer names a form of the game itself.

clue.text: Affected Reform UK, say, with head removed

indicators.note: Say marks what comes before it as an example, so the word wanted is the general class the named thing belongs to.
Removed means taken away, so the letter named beside it does not appear in the answer.

parts.note: Reform UK is one of Britain's political parties, the one Nigel Farage leads
the head of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Reform UK putting on airs now that its leader has been got rid of.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' is the flag that Reform UK is only an instance of the word wanted, a device worth spotting early because it never contributes letters of its own. Arty means affected about art, the pose rather than the ability.
explanation.definitionFit: Somebody arty makes a show of artistic taste, which is affectation rather than art, and affected is the word for that pose.

clue.text: See 17 Down
See 27 Across
Pool party after nude hen night not new

indicators.note: After sends the word in front of it to the back, so the party finishes the entry rather than starting it.
Nude is with the clothes off, so the word loses the letters on its outside and only its middle is left.

parts.note: the middle letter, once the outer two are stripped away

indicators.note: Not takes away what it names, so that letter is missing from the word standing before it.

parts.note: five letters, the word the deletion works on
n is the standard abbreviation for new
a formal dance, the grandest sort of party

explanation.surface: A pool party following a hen night that nobody bothered to get dressed for.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pool party' looks like one phrase and is two jobs — the definition, then a word that only has to mean ball. Eight-ball is the pub game in which the black goes down last, and the black itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Eight-ball is the form of pool played on pub tables everywhere, named for the black ball that has to be sunk at the end.

clue.text: More graceful win; limper member abandoned

parts.note: to gain is to win — ground, time, an advantage

indicators.note: What has been abandoned has been left behind, so the letters named are dropped from the word in front.

parts.note: six letters, the word the deletion works on
a Member of Parliament is an MP, and members is what the Commons calls them

explanation.surface: A victory looking better once the hobbling member has dropped out of the race.
explanation.walkthrough: Gainly is the word 'ungainly' was built from, still in the dictionary and almost never said aloud, which is why the comparative looks so odd. The semicolon is punctuation, not instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Gainly means shapely or graceful, the positive that survives mainly inside its own negative, so gainlier is more graceful.
